accounting-fundamentals--exp-c5-sc3.prompt: In a closed month, 900 of utilities was posted to Rent Expense by mistake. Judged by audit-trail criteria, which fix is best?

options.label: Overwrite the amount in the Rent Expense ledger by hand so that the account totals now agree with the invoice and the books balance
Leave it as is, since both are expenses and net income is unaffected, and note the misclassification in the next period's review
Delete the original line and re-enter it to Utilities Expense so the ledger only ever shows the correct posting for that closed month
Post a dated correcting entry debiting Utilities Expense and crediting Rent Expense 900, with a note

rubric: A dated correcting entry keeps the original record and shows what changed and why.
Deleting or overwriting destroys the trail; ignoring it leaves individual expense accounts wrong.

accounting-fundamentals--nov-c2-sc4.prompt: A journal entry shows a credit to the Cash account of $200. What does this mean?

options.label: The business owes $200 to a lender
Cash was recorded twice by mistake
The business received $200 in cash
Cash decreased by $200

rubric: Credits decrease asset accounts, so Cash fell by $200.
Learners often read credit as 'money in', which is a common everyday confusion.

agile-scrum--adb-c3-sc4.prompt: In a retrospective, a team notes its Daily Scrum often runs 30 minutes because of long technical debates. Which action best applies Scrum practice?

options.label: Keep it to 15 minutes and take deep talks to a follow-up
Have the Scrum Master run it and decide who may speak and for how long each time
Invite stakeholders so the debates are settled in front of them, then record decisions
Cancel the Daily Scrum and replace it with a weekly written report from each member

rubric: The Daily Scrum is timeboxed to 15 minutes; detailed talks happen afterwards.
Other options remove the event, shift ownership or add the wrong audience.

agile-scrum--cmp-c3-sn1.prompt: A team uses a Kanban board with a WIP limit of 4 on the 'In Review' column, and it currently holds 4 items. A developer finishes coding a ticket and is ready to move it forward. The backlog has plenty of ready tickets. What should the developer do?

options.label: Raise the review limit to 5 for now, since the finished ticket is already done coding and shouldn't sit idle
Leave the ticket in Coding and pick up a lower-priority bug fix, so the developer stays busy while review clears
Pull the next ticket from the backlog, since coding capacity is free and the review limit only applies to reviewers
Help review one of the four waiting items so the queue drains

rubric: WIP limits push the team to finish work before starting more, so swarming on review is right.
Raising the limit or starting new work hides the bottleneck.

algebra--adb-c2-sc5.prompt: Two lines in a system have the same slope but different y-intercepts. How many solutions does the system have?

options.label: None
Infinitely many
Exactly two
Exactly one

rubric: Parallel lines never intersect, so there is no solution.
Distractors confuse parallel lines with intersecting or identical lines.

algebra--nov-c2-sc1.prompt: Why can you add the same number to both sides of an equation without changing its solution?

options.label: It moves the variable term to the other side, which isolates it
Both sides stay equal, so the balance is preserved
It shrinks the numbers on the left side, so the equation is simpler
It turns the equation into an inequality with the same solutions

rubric: Equality is preserved when equal amounts are added to equal quantities.
Distractors confuse the purpose with simplifying or moving terms.

algorithms--nov-c1-sc2.prompt: Which precondition must hold for binary search to work on an array?

options.label: The array must be sorted
The array must have an even length
The array must contain no duplicates
The array must contain only integers

rubric: Binary search relies on sorted order to discard half.
Distractors add unrelated requirements.

algorithms--nov-c2-sc2.prompt: What happens if a recursive function has no base case?

options.label: The compiler converts it into a loop that runs until the input is empty
It returns zero or null after the first call, since nothing is left to do
It keeps calling itself until the stack overflows
It runs once and then stops, since the second call finds no work

rubric: Without a base case, calls pile up until overflow.
Distractors assume automatic stopping.

astronomy--exp-c5-sc4.prompt: You want an Earth-size candidate's radius and a first look at its atmosphere, and its orbit is known to be edge-on. Which detection method serves best?

options.label: Transit photometry, since depth gives radius and filtered starlight carries spectra
Gravitational microlensing, since the lensing light curve gives the planet's mass ratio and separation even for planets in any orbital alignment
Radial velocity monitoring, since the stellar Doppler shift gives a precise minimum mass for planets orbiting close to the star
Direct imaging with a coronagraph, since blocking the star's glare lets the planet's own thermal light be resolved and analysed

rubric: Transits give radius from depth, and transmission spectroscopy reads the atmosphere when the orbit is edge-on.
Radial velocity gives mass, imaging struggles with Earth-size planets, and microlensing events do not repeat for follow-up.

astronomy--nov-c1-sc5.prompt: Which unit of length is defined by how far a beam of light travels through space in one Earth year?

options.label: Light-year
Parsec, the distance at which one AU subtends one arcsecond
Solar radius, the distance from the Sun's center to its visible surface
Astronomical unit, the average distance from Earth to the Sun

rubric: A light-year is the distance light travels in a year.
The astronomical unit is the Earth-Sun distance, often confused.

asynchronous-javascript--adb-c2-sc5.prompt: What does an `async` function return when its body ends with `return 42;`?

options.label: The number 42, unchanged, available immediately to the caller
undefined, unless the function body contains an await
A callback function that the caller must invoke to get 42
A promise that fulfils with the value 42

rubric: Async functions always wrap their return value in a promise.
Choosing the plain number ignores the automatic promise wrapping.

asynchronous-javascript--exp-c6-sc4.prompt: Existing code: `const a = loadA(); const b = loadB(); const x = await a; const y = await b;`. New requirements: both calls start immediately, any failure is handled in one catch, and no unhandled-rejection warning even if `b` fails first. Which rewrite meets them?

options.label: Keep the code and add `await Promise.resolve()` between the lines so any rejection is observed before it can be reported
`try { const x = await loadA(); const y = await loadB(); } catch (e) { /* handle */ }`, so each await is handled in turn
`try { const [x, y] = await Promise.all([loadA(), loadB()]); } catch (e) { /* handle */ }`
Keep the code and wrap those four lines in one try/catch, since the catch will handle the rejection of both promises

rubric: `Promise.all` attaches handlers to both promises immediately, so an early rejection of `b` is handled once.
In the original, `b` has no handler while `a` is awaited, so try/catch alone does not prevent the warning; sequential awaits break parallelism.

authentication-authorization--adb-c2-sn1.prompt: A team issues JWT access tokens valid for 24 hours and validates them on every API call. A user logs out, but a copy of their old token still works for the API the next hour. Why does this happen?

options.label: The server checks only signature and expiry, so nothing marks the token revoked
The signature stays valid after logout because the server only re-signs tokens when the user logs in again
Logout deletes the token from the database, but a cache keeps serving the stale copy until it is refreshed
JWTs are bound to the user's IP address at login, and that address has not changed since the user signed in

rubric: Stateless validation checks only signature and expiry, so logout does not invalidate the token.
Distractors invent server storage, IP binding, or odd signature behaviour.

authentication-authorization--adb-c3-sc1.prompt: A login handler has just verified a user's password. A visitor's pre-login session ID was set earlier. To prevent session fixation, what should the handler do next?

options.label: Keep the pre-login session ID and copy the cart into it, so the user's cart is preserved
Keep the pre-login session ID but mark it as authenticated and set the HttpOnly flag on its cookie
Extend the old session's expiry to 30 days so the user is not logged out
Issue a new session ID and discard the pre-login one

rubric: Regenerating the session ID at login stops an attacker reusing a known ID.
Distractors keep or extend the old ID, which leaves fixation possible.

authentication-authorization--cmp-c4-sc3.prompt: An OAuth provider accepts any redirect_uri that begins with https://app.example.com, and attackers obtain victims' authorization codes. Which step in the flow is faulty?

options.label: Redirect URI is prefix-matched, so https://app.example.com.evil.net gets the code
The consent screen is skipped for returning users, so attackers can bypass the approval step and obtain codes
The token endpoint accepts the client ID without a secret, so attackers can exchange codes they have intercepted
Authorization codes travel in the query string, which exposes them to anyone who can read the browser's address bar

rubric: Redirect URIs must be compared by exact match; prefix matching lets lookalike hosts receive codes.
The other options misattribute the leak to normal protocol features.

authentication-authorization--exp-c5-sc2.prompt: A public single-page app has no place to keep a secret and is used on shared kiosks. Criteria: resist authorization-code interception and avoid exposing access tokens in URLs. Which OAuth approach is best?

options.label: Authorization code flow with a client secret embedded in the bundle, since the secret authenticates the app to the token endpoint
Resource owner password credentials flow, since the app collects credentials itself and avoids redirect interception entirely
Authorization code flow with PKCE, so an intercepted code is useless without the verifier
Implicit flow, because the access token returns directly in the redirect and no code exchange exists to intercept

rubric: PKCE binds the code to a verifier held by the client, suiting public clients.
Implicit puts tokens in URLs, an embedded secret is extractable, and the password grant exposes credentials to the app.

aws--cmp-c3-sn1.prompt: An Auto Scaling group has 4 instances and a target tracking policy of 50% average CPU. Traffic rises and average CPU reaches 75%. Max size is 10. Roughly what will the group do?

options.label: Scale out straight to the maximum of 10, since any breach launches the full capacity
Scale out to about 6 instances to bring CPU near 50%
Do nothing until CPU exceeds 90%, since policies wait for a large breach
Add one instance per cycle until the alarm clears, like simple scaling

rubric: Target tracking scales proportionally: 4 x 75/50 = 6.
Others misunderstand direction or ignore proportional scaling.

aws--cmp-c4-sc2.prompt: A Lambda function in private subnets of a VPC times out when calling DynamoDB, but works when not attached to a VPC. The subnets have no NAT gateway. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The execution role lacks dynamodb:GetItem permission, so DynamoDB silently drops the requests until they time out
The function has no network path to DynamoDB's public endpoint
The function's security group blocks inbound traffic from DynamoDB, so the responses to its calls never arrive
DynamoDB tables must be in the same subnet as the function, and the table sits outside the private subnets

rubric: VPC-attached Lambda needs a NAT or a gateway VPC endpoint to reach DynamoDB.
Missing IAM permission yields an AccessDenied error, not a timeout.

bayesian-statistics--nov-c2-sc4.prompt: Which statement best describes how a Bayesian credible interval differs from a frequentist confidence interval in interpretation?

options.label: The credible interval is usually narrower, because it uses the same data more efficiently
The credible interval does not depend on a prior, so it is more objective than a confidence interval
The credible interval describes the long-run share of repeated samples whose intervals contain the parameter
The credible interval gives the probability the parameter lies in it

rubric: A credible interval gives the probability the parameter lies in it, given data and prior.
A confidence interval describes long-run coverage of the procedure, not the parameter's probability.

biochemistry--cmp-c4-sc3.prompt: A mutation replaces a buried leucine in a protein's core with aspartate, and the protein loses activity. Which analysis best explains this?

options.label: Aspartate is larger than leucine, so its bulk sterically blocks the active site and prevents substrate from binding
Leucine is required for peptide bond formation at that position, so the chain cannot be extended past the mutation
A charged residue in the hydrophobic core disrupts packing and destabilises folding
Aspartate has no matching tRNA synthetase, so the ribosome cannot incorporate it and truncated protein forms

rubric: A charged side chain buried in a nonpolar core is unfavourable and destabilises the fold.
Aspartate is normally incorporated and is smaller than leucine; the other options are factually wrong.

biochemistry--exp-c5-sc3.prompt: A student states that the rate-limiting step of a pathway is simply the enzyme catalysing the reaction with the most negative ΔG. Using metabolic control analysis, which evaluation is best?

options.label: Flawed: control always sits with the enzyme with the highest Km, because substrate affinity alone sets the rate of the pathway and the other steps only follow it
Sound: the most exergonic step is the slowest step, so the enzyme there fixes the flux and all other enzymes in the pathway have zero control over it
Flawed: far-from-equilibrium steps are candidates, but control is shared and measured by flux control coefficients
Sound: a large negative ΔG means the step is irreversible, and irreversible steps alone are able to control the flux of a pathway under all conditions

rubric: Metabolic control analysis shows flux control is distributed and measured experimentally; ΔG only flags candidates.
Distractors keep the single rate-limiting-step dogma or substitute Km for control.

biochemistry--prf-c5-sc5.prompt: Which justification best supports calling PFK-1, rather than hexokinase, the main control point of glycolysis?

options.label: It catalyses the first committed, irreversible step and is tuned allosterically by ATP, AMP and F2,6BP
It is the only glycolytic enzyme that consumes ATP in the pathway, so its rate directly sets the rate of every other step downstream
It has the highest kcat of all the glycolytic enzymes, so even small changes in its activity are greatly amplified through the pathway
It operates near equilibrium in the cell, so small changes in substrate levels can readily reverse its direction and throttle flux

rubric: PFK-1 is the committed step, far from equilibrium, and responds to energy signals.
Hexokinase also consumes ATP, and a near-equilibrium enzyme is a poor control point.

business-law--cmp-c3-sc3.prompt: A freelance designer creates a logo for a client under a one-page agreement that says nothing about ownership. No employment relationship exists. Applying the usual default rule, who owns the copyright in the logo?

options.label: Both jointly, because both contributed creative and commercial input to the final result
The client, because the logo will be used in the client's business and carries its brand
The designer, unless it is assigned in writing to the client
The client, because the client paid the full agreed fee for the finished work

rubric: An independent contractor generally keeps copyright unless there is a written assignment.
Distractors assume payment or use transfers ownership.

business-law--cmp-c4-sn1.prompt: A bakery owner hired a baker who signed a non-compete barring work at any bakery worldwide for ten years. The baker is dismissed and opens a stall across town. The owner wants a court order stopping her. Which analysis best predicts the outcome?

options.label: A court will void it entirely, because restrictions on working after leaving a job are against public policy and never enforceable
A court will enforce it in full, because the baker signed voluntarily and a signed contract is binding as written in every respect
A court will enforce it, because dismissal by the employer removes the baker's defences and leaves the restriction fully in force
A court may refuse enforcement, since the scope and duration exceed what protects legitimate interests

rubric: Non-competes are generally enforced only if reasonable in scope, time and geography.
Distractors treat signature as decisive or assume blanket invalidity.

business-law--exp-c6-sc3.prompt: A startup's plan for handling customers' personal data includes a privacy notice, a cookie banner and database encryption. Which addition fills the most important gap in the design?

options.label: A stronger encryption algorithm for the database, since security of stored data is the main duty and other privacy obligations follow from it
A retained outside privacy lawyer who reviews each product release, since regulators expect legal sign-off before any data is collected
A data inventory of personal data held and vendors receiving it, with written data-processing contracts
A consent pop-up on every page that asks users to accept all processing, since consent is the lawful basis for all personal data use

rubric: Knowing what data is held and where it flows, and papering vendor processing, underpins compliance.
Distractors treat technology, trademarks or headcount as substitutes for mapping data and vendor contracts.

business-strategy--exp-c5-sc4.prompt: Porter warns firms against being 'stuck in the middle' between cost leadership and differentiation. Where does that advice most likely break down?

options.label: When a new process or technology cuts cost and raises quality together, so differentiation adds little cost
When the industry is mature and price competition squeezes margins, because any differentiation then becomes unprofitable and the firm must hold a blended position
When customers are highly price sensitive, because they reward a firm that blends low price with moderate quality over a pure cost leader
When the firm is small and lacks scale, because only large firms can afford differentiation, so a smaller firm must blend both positions

rubric: The trade-off assumption fails when innovation shifts the cost-quality frontier.
Distractors cite maturity, size or price sensitivity, which do not remove the trade-off.

business-strategy--exp-c5-sn1.prompt: Your firm has high fixed costs and 80% of its customers value service over price. A smaller rival cuts prices 15% to target the price-sensitive 20% of your volume. Your goal is to protect total profit. Which response is best?

options.label: Cut prices 30% across the range to punish the rival, since a deeper cut signals resolve and deters further entry
Hold core prices and offer a limited low-price product to the exposed segment
Match the 15% cut across all products, since high fixed costs make every lost unit of volume costly to absorb
Ignore the move and hold all prices, since a smaller rival cannot sustain lower prices for long and will soon exit

rubric: Targeted response protects the core margin while defending the exposed segment.
Distractors either give away margin on loyal customers, assume exit, or escalate the price war.

business-writing--cmp-c3-sc3.prompt: You are emailing 30 staff to submit timesheets by 5 pm this Thursday. Which subject line works best?

options.label: Timesheet policy update: please read the attached submission process before the end of the week
Reminder from Payroll about the timesheet cutoff and what happens when entries arrive late
Action needed: submit timesheets by 5 pm Thursday
Timesheets, please: payroll runs soon and we need everyone's hours entered correctly

rubric: The key states the action and deadline, so readers can act even without opening the email.
Distractors are vague, omit the deadline or signal information rather than a required action.

business-writing--nov-c1-sc2.prompt: In the direct approach to business writing, where does the main point or request normally go?

options.label: At the start
After all background
In the closing line
In the signature block

rubric: The direct approach states the main point first, then gives support.
Distractors reflect the habit of building up to the point, which is the indirect approach.

business-writing--nov-c2-sn1.prompt: A team lead emails colleagues in three time zones: 'Please send me the figures ASAP.' Replies arrive over three days, and several people say they were unsure how urgent it was. What is the best explanation and fix?

options.label: A written request is too blunt without a deadline; ask for the figures 'when convenient' to stay polite
ASAP means different things to different readers; give a date and time
The email is too short to convey urgency; add several sentences explaining why the figures matter
ASAP is too formal for colleagues in other offices; use 'whenever you can' so replies feel relaxed

rubric: Vague urgency terms are read differently; a specific date and time removes doubt.
Distractors misdiagnose the problem as formality, length or the presence of deadlines.

calculus--cmp-c4-sc3.prompt: A student claims the Mean Value Theorem for f(x) = |x| on [-1, 2] gives a point c with f'(c) = 1/3, but no such c exists. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: The theorem only holds for intervals that start at 0, and this one starts at -1
The average rate of change is 1, not 1/3, so the student's computation is wrong
f is not continuous at x = 0 inside the interval, so the theorem does not apply
f is not differentiable at x = 0, so the hypotheses fail

rubric: |x| is continuous but not differentiable at 0; its slope is only +1 or -1, so 1/3 is never attained, and the MVT hypotheses fail.
Distractors blame continuity, the arithmetic (the average slope is (2 - 1)/3 = 1/3), or an invented restriction.

calculus--cmp-c4-sn1.prompt: A factory's total cost is C(x) = 0.5x^2 + 200 for x units. An analyst finds that average cost A(x) = C(x)/x is smallest where marginal cost C'(x) equals A(x). A colleague asks why this condition must hold at a minimum of A. Which reasoning is correct?

options.label: C(x) is smallest at that output, so its slope C'(x) must equal the average cost there
Fixed costs vanish at the minimum of A, so C'(x) and A(x) must coincide at that output
A'(x) = (xC'(x) - C(x))/x^2, zero exactly when C'(x) = C(x)/x
Marginal cost always equals average cost for any cost function, so it holds at every output level

rubric: The quotient rule gives A' = (xC' - C)/x^2; setting A' = 0 gives C' = C/x (here x = 20).
Distractors treat the equality as universal, confuse minimising C with minimising A, or invoke fixed costs vanishing.

calculus--exp-c6-sc5.prompt: A colleague 'proves' that every continuous f on the open interval (0,1) is bounded by citing the Extreme Value Theorem. Which added hypothesis repairs the argument with minimal change?

options.label: f is monotonic on (0,1), since a monotonic function is bounded by its values at the two endpoints of the interval.
f is differentiable on (0,1), since differentiability supplies the compactness that the theorem requires on the interval.
f extends continuously to [0,1], so finite limits exist at both endpoints.
f is integrable on (0,1), since a finite area forces the function values to stay bounded near both endpoints.

rubric: The theorem needs a closed bounded interval; a continuous extension to [0,1] provides it.
Differentiability, monotonicity and integrability do not prevent blow-up, as 1/x shows.

chemical-equilibrium--exp-c5-sc2.prompt: For A ⇌ I (rate constants k1, k-1) followed by I → P (k2), a chemist wants to use the pre-equilibrium approximation, rate = k2K[A]. Which rate-constant set best justifies it?

options.label: k1 = 1e6 s^-1 and k-1 = 1e2 s^-1, because a large forward constant means step 1 reaches equilibrium before any I can react further
k-1 = 1e6 s^-1 and k2 = 1e2 s^-1, because I reverts to A far faster than it forms P
k-1 = 1e4 s^-1 and k2 = 1e4 s^-1, because equal rate constants mean I returns to A as often as it goes on to P
k-1 = 1e2 s^-1 and k2 = 1e6 s^-1, because I forms P so quickly that the first step is held at equilibrium by it

rubric: Pre-equilibrium requires k-1 much greater than k2 so step 1 is not drained by step 2.
Distractors reverse the inequality, assume equal constants suffice, or confuse a large K with fast equilibration.

ci-cd--adb-c3-sn1.prompt: A workflow has jobs `test` and `deploy`, with no `needs` setting. A pull request has failing tests, yet the deploy job still ran and shipped the change. The team wants deploy to run only when tests pass. What should you change?

options.label: Add `needs: test` to the deploy job so it waits for a passing test job
Add a `timeout-minutes` limit to the deploy job so it is cancelled if tests take too long to finish
Move the deploy commands into the last step of the test job so both run in the same runner environment
Set `continue-on-error: true` on the test job so a failing test no longer blocks later jobs in the run

rubric: Without `needs`, jobs run in parallel; `needs: test` makes deploy depend on test success.
Other options hide failures, mix concerns or add manual steps instead of declaring the dependency.

classical-mechanics--cmp-c4-sc5.prompt: A satellite is moved from a low circular orbit to a higher circular orbit. Its speed decreases, yet its total mechanical energy increases. How can both be true?

options.label: Potential energy rises by more than kinetic energy falls, so the total rises even though speed drops
Gravity is weaker at the higher orbit, so the satellite does less work against it and its kinetic energy is converted into total energy
Kinetic energy and potential energy both increase at the higher orbit, so the lower speed is an apparent effect of the changing reference frame
Potential energy falls at the greater distance because gravity is weaker there, and the loss is outweighed by the kinetic energy gained

rubric: Kinetic energy is GMm/2r, which falls, while total energy -GMm/2r rises toward zero because potential energy rises more.
Distractors misread the energy bookkeeping or invoke continuous thrust.

classical-mechanics--exp-c5-sc5.prompt: An astronaut in a circular orbit wants to reach a tool floating ahead of her in the same orbit. Which plan is best?

options.label: Thrust radially outward; this adds no speed along the orbit, so her path stays circular and closes the gap directly
Thrust backward to drop to a lower, faster orbit, then re-raise it once the gap closes
Thrust forward along the orbit; the extra speed carries her toward the tool faster along the same circular path
Thrust forward to gain speed and coast; the higher orbit she enters has a shorter period, so she sweeps around to the tool sooner

rubric: A retrograde burn lowers the orbit, shortening the period so she gains on the tool.
Distractors apply straight-line intuition that more forward speed closes the gap.

classical-mechanics--nov-c2-sc1.prompt: A hockey puck slides on frictionless ice at constant velocity. What does Newton's first law say about the net force on it?

options.label: It slowly decreases
It is zero
It equals the puck's weight
It points along the motion

rubric: Constant velocity means zero net force.
Many learners think motion needs a force in the direction of travel.

classical-mechanics--nov-c2-sc2.prompt: A ball is thrown straight up. At the very top of its path, ignoring air resistance, what is its acceleration?

options.label: Undefined, because the ball is momentarily at rest
9.8 m/s^2 downward
9.8 m/s^2 upward, matching the throw direction
Zero, because its velocity is zero there

rubric: Gravity acts throughout, so acceleration stays 9.8 m/s^2 downward.
Zero velocity at the top is mistaken for zero acceleration.

options.label: Fixing bugs found in production by changing how the code behaves
Restructuring code without changing its behavior
Speeding up slow code so that it can handle much larger inputs
Adding new features by rewriting old code to behave differently

rubric: Refactoring restructures code while keeping observable behavior the same.
Distractors confuse it with feature work, bug fixing, or performance tuning, which all change behavior or aim at something else.

clean-code-refactoring--cmp-c3-sc2.prompt: A function is written as `def f(d, n): return d + timedelta(days=n)`. Which name and parameter list best express what it does and keep call sites clear?

options.label: `add_days(start_date, days)`
`shift_date(start_date, offset)`, where offset is a day count
`get_new_date(start_date, number_of_days)` for the resulting date
`update_date(date_value, days)`, changing the date it receives

rubric: `add_days(date, days)` names the operation and its inputs precisely.
Distractors use vague verbs such as get, process or calculate that say nothing about what happens.

climate-science--adb-c2-sc4.prompt: A region has an unusually cold week in winter. What does this event most reasonably show about climate?

options.label: It shows greenhouse gases have stopped trapping heat in that region
It shows that the long-term global warming trend has paused for now
It is normal weather variability, not a climate trend
It shows the climate of that region has begun shifting toward cooling

rubric: Climate is the average over decades, so one cold week is weather variability.
Distractors treat a short local event as a trend or as a change in physics.

climate-science--adb-c2-sn1.prompt: A news report says the average pH of the ocean surface has fallen over the past century as CO2 has risen. A student asks why more atmospheric CO2 would make seawater more acidic. Which explanation is correct?

options.label: Dissolved CO2 forms carbonic acid, which releases hydrogen ions
Extra CO2 traps heat that warms the surface water, and the warmer water always has a lower pH
CO2 reacts with the chloride in seawater salt to form hydrochloric acid directly
CO2 displaces dissolved oxygen from the water, and the oxygen loss makes the water acidic

rubric: CO2 + H2O forms carbonic acid, which dissociates and adds hydrogen ions, lowering pH.
Distractors invent hydrochloric acid, overstate temperature effects, or blame oxygen loss.

climate-science--exp-c6-sc2.prompt: You need Eocene tropical sea-surface temperatures from a deep-sea core below the carbonate compensation depth, so the sediment contains no carbonate. Which proxy design fits these constraints?

options.label: Sr/Ca ratios measured in preserved coral skeletons
δ18O measured on planktonic foraminiferal shells
TEX86 from archaeal membrane lipids
Mg/Ca ratios measured in foraminiferal calcite

rubric: TEX86 uses organic lipids that survive without carbonate and records sea-surface temperature.
The other proxies need carbonate shells or coral, which this core lacks.

climate-science--nov-c1-sc1.prompt: Which gas is the largest contributor to human-caused warming through its rising concentration in the atmosphere?

options.label: Water vapour from oceans
Carbon dioxide
Methane from livestock
Nitrous oxide from soils

rubric: CO2 from fossil fuels and land use is the largest driver of human-caused warming.
Nitrogen and oxygen make up most of air but do not absorb infrared radiation significantly.

options.label: Running all workloads on virtual machines rented from a single public cloud provider
Using two different public SaaS products, such as separate email and chat services
Hosting all servers in a company's own data center with no outside cloud services
Combining private infrastructure with public cloud services

rubric: Hybrid combines private and public environments.
Using several SaaS apps or one provider is not hybrid.

cognitive-biases--adb-c3-sc5.prompt: A nurse thinks full moons make the emergency room busier. To test this fairly without confirmation bias, which records should she review?

options.label: Every night, full moon or not, busy or quiet
Only full-moon nights, noting how busy each one was in the ER
The nights she remembers best, since the vivid ones stand out most
Only the busiest nights, to see how many fell on a full moon

rubric: A fair test counts all four combinations, including cases that would disconfirm the belief.
The other options use selected or memorable cases only.

cognitive-biases--cmp-c4-sc5.prompt: In a study, people spin a wheel that lands on 10 or 65, then estimate the percentage of African countries in the UN. Those who saw 65 give higher estimates. Which feature of this result shows anchoring rather than relevant knowledge?

options.label: A random wheel number still pulled estimates toward itself
Both groups' average estimates fell above the true value, which shows a general overestimation tendency
Participants gave percentages rather than counts, which forced them to rely on rough guesses
Estimates within each group varied widely, which shows that people used different knowledge

rubric: An uninformative number that still shifts judgments is the signature of anchoring.
Other features do not link the estimates to the arbitrary number.

cognitive-biases--exp-c6-sn1.prompt: A news app finds that users who read a story about a rare local crime overestimate how common crime is nearby. The team wants a feature that gives a calibrated view. Constraints: no lectures, honest content, low friction. Which design meets all of them?

options.label: Show a small chart of local crime rates per capita beside the story, as a base-rate reference.
Show a pop-up explaining availability bias and asking users to avoid it before they are allowed to open the story, so they read with the bias in mind.
Hide stories about rare crimes so users are no longer exposed to vivid cases that distort how common crime seems in their area.
Add emotional language to stories about safe events so they become as memorable as stories about rare crimes and balance recall.

rubric: A base-rate display counters availability at the moment of judgement, honestly and with little friction.
Pop-ups lecture, hiding stories is not honest reporting, and emotional embellishment is manipulative.

cognitive-biases--nov-c2-sc2.prompt: A manager decides early that a new hire is weak. For weeks she remembers every mistake the hire makes and overlooks the successes. Which bias is this?

options.label: Confirmation bias
Availability bias from a vivid news story
Hindsight bias after a project fails
Anchoring on the first salary figure

rubric: She notices and remembers evidence that fits her existing belief.
Other options do not match: no number, no known outcome, no news-driven examples.

cognitive-biases--prf-c5-sc1.prompt: You must reply at once to a seller's very high opening price. Your criteria are low cost, usable in the meeting and resistance to anchoring. Which approach best meets them?

options.label: Counter within a fair-value range prepared beforehand from comparables
Stay silent and wait for the seller to make further concessions before you form any view of a fair price
Tell yourself to ignore the seller's number, then judge the price by gut feeling about what seems fair
Offer the midpoint between your budget and the seller's price, to show goodwill and keep talks moving

rubric: An independent, pre-set reference range counters the anchor without extra cost during the meeting.
Simply trying to ignore an anchor is weak, and splitting the difference stays tied to the seller's inflated number.

cognitive-biases--prf-c5-sn1.prompt: An emergency department finds clinicians often keep their first diagnosis despite new findings. Management wants a fix that costs little, fits a five-minute handoff and does not ban intuition. Which intervention best fits these criteria?

options.label: Send clinicians to an annual lecture on cognitive biases and diagnostic errors in emergency care
Delay any working diagnosis until the main test results are back, so early impressions cannot anchor
Add a handoff prompt: "What else could this be, and what doesn't fit?"
Have a second specialist review most diagnoses before treatment begins, to catch anchoring errors

rubric: A brief consider-the-alternatives prompt is cheap, fits the time limit and leaves intuition intact while countering anchoring.
Universal second reviews are costly, lectures transfer weakly, and banning early impressions is impractical and loses their value.

compilers-interpreters--nov-c2-sn1.prompt: A team wants one build of its program to run on both Windows and Linux without recompiling for each. They compile the source to bytecode and ship a virtual machine for each operating system. Why does this approach meet their goal?

options.label: The bytecode skips lexing and parsing on each machine, so no OS-specific work is left
Windows and Linux share one CPU instruction set, so the bytecode runs natively on both
Each VM turns the same bytecode into actions on its own platform
The bytecode is rewritten as source on each machine and then compiled again to native code

rubric: Bytecode is platform-neutral; each platform's VM handles the machine-specific work.
Distractors misunderstand what bytecode is or what the VM does.

computer-networking--cmp-c4-sc3.prompt: Host A is `192.168.1.10/24` and host B is `192.168.2.10/24`. Both plug into the same unmanaged switch with no router, and they cannot ping each other. Why?

options.label: Each host sees the other as off-subnet and needs a gateway that is absent
The switch ports negotiated different speeds, so the link between the hosts cannot carry frames
A /24 mask is only valid on routed links, so the switch refuses to forward frames between those hosts
The hosts' MAC addresses fall in the same vendor range, so the switch treats them as duplicates and drops frames

rubric: Different subnets require a router; the switch forwards frames by MAC and does not route between IP subnets.
Being on the same physical switch does not put hosts in the same IP subnet.

concurrency-parallelism--adb-c2-sc5.prompt: What does a mutex (mutual exclusion lock) guarantee?

options.label: Waiting threads are released in the order they were created
Only one thread holds it at a time
Guarded variables become private copies for every thread
Guarded code runs faster because it is pinned to one core

rubric: A mutex enforces exclusive access to a critical section.
Distractors attribute speed, ordering or copying to locks, which they do not provide.

concurrency-parallelism--cmp-c4-sc3.prompt: A CPU-bound service on 4 cores ran well with 4 worker threads. Raising to 64 threads that share one lock made throughput drop. What best explains this?

options.label: The OS limits each process to about one runnable thread per core, so the extra threads sit blocked and add scheduler bookkeeping overhead
Extra runnable threads add context switching and lock contention but no compute
Extra threads make each critical section run longer because the lock itself slows down as more waiters queue up on it
Threads beyond the core count cannot be scheduled until the first four finish, so the extra threads only consume memory and stall

rubric: Oversubscription adds switching and lock-queue overhead while the cores were already saturated.
The other options invent OS limits or scheduling rules that do not exist.

concurrency-parallelism--nov-c1-sc5.prompt: Which definition describes parallelism, as opposed to mere concurrency?

options.label: Tasks executing at the same instant on multiple cores
Tasks that are written in separate source files and then compiled together
Tasks that never need to share any data or wait for any other task to finish
Tasks that take turns on one core so that each makes progress over time

rubric: Parallelism means simultaneous execution on multiple processing units.
The third distractor describes concurrency by time-slicing.

concurrency-parallelism--nov-c2-sc4.prompt: Why does making every thread acquire locks A and B in the same fixed order prevent deadlock?

options.label: It stops the scheduler from switching threads while any lock is held, so no thread is paused mid-wait
It removes circular wait, so no cycle of waiting threads can form
It lets two threads hold the same lock at once, so neither has to wait for the other
It makes each lock release itself after a short time limit, so waiting threads never block forever

rubric: Consistent ordering breaks the circular-wait condition.
Distractors describe timeouts, shared holding or disabling the scheduler.

conflict-resolution--adb-c2-sc5.prompt: A manager hears one employee's side of a dispute and immediately rules in that person's favour without hearing the other. What is the most likely result?

options.label: The other employee trusts the manager's fairness because a clear ruling was given
The dispute ends quickly because the manager's authority settles it for both
The other employee feels unheard and resentment continues
Both employees accept the outcome because it was made quickly and decisively

rubric: Skipping one party's account leaves them feeling unheard and fuels hidden resentment.
Distractors assume that speed or authority creates acceptance.

control-systems--nov-c2-sn1.prompt: A car's cruise control uses proportional feedback. After a step in set speed, the speed overshoots slightly and settles. An engineer doubles then quadruples the gain, and the speed now oscillates with growing amplitude. What best explains this?

options.label: Higher gain pushed the loop past its stability limit
The set speed is too far from the starting speed, so the error is too large
Sensor noise has increased in proportion to the gain and is being amplified
The actuator saturated and stopped responding to the controller's commands

rubric: Raising gain can push poles across the imaginary axis, causing growing oscillation, i.e. instability.
The loop is proportional only, so integral saturation does not apply, and noise would not cause smooth growth.

cooking-fundamentals--cmp-c3-sn1.prompt: Your recipe roasts a 1.5 kg chicken at 200C for 70 minutes. The bird you bought weighs 2.2 kg. You want it cooked through with moist meat. What is the best approach?

options.label: Roast longer than 70 minutes and check the thigh reaches 74C
Roast at 230C for 70 minutes so the larger bird finishes in the same time as the recipe
Roast 70 minutes, then judge by whether the skin looks golden brown and crisp all over
Multiply the time exactly by 2.2/1.5 and skip any further checks on the meat

rubric: A larger bird needs more time, and internal temperature is the reliable measure of doneness.
Distractors rely on a fixed time, a hotter oven or surface colour.

cooking-fundamentals--nov-c2-sc4.prompt: A recipe says to 'preheat the oven to 200°C.' What is the main reason for this step?

options.label: Food starts cooking at the right temperature, so timing and browning work
Food dries out less when the oven is already hot before it goes in, since it spends less time inside
The recipe time is counted only after the oven has cooled slightly from its peak, so the food does not scorch
The oven needs to burn off food residue from earlier use before it can safely cook anything new

rubric: Preheating makes the recipe's timing reliable.
Other options are myths about residue or cooling.

cooking-fundamentals--prf-c4-sc2.prompt: A whole roast chicken comes out with dry breast meat, yet the thighs are still slightly pink at the bone when the breast hits its target temperature. What best explains the mismatch?

options.label: The breast's skin is thinner than the thigh's, so it cooks faster, and removing the breast skin before roasting would even out the timing
The thighs sit lower in the oven, so hotter air reaches the breast first and cooks the breast unevenly while the thighs stay cooler
Lean breast is done at a lower temperature, while collagen-rich thighs need higher heat to turn tender
The thighs hold more water, so they absorb oven heat more slowly and always lag behind the breast, whatever the final temperature

rubric: Lean breast and collagen-rich thighs have different ideal finishing temperatures, so one oven time fits only one.
Distractors invent oven-position or skin explanations rather than muscle composition.

copywriting--adb-c3-sc4.prompt: You are using the Problem-Agitate-Solve formula. You've written: 'Your emails go unread and sales stall.' What should come next?

options.label: Show what staying stuck will cost the reader
Add a customer testimonial and a star rating to build trust
Close with a countdown deadline and a button to create urgency
Offer the product at once and state its price and benefits

rubric: After stating the problem, PAS deepens the felt consequences before the solution.
Other options skip the agitation step and jump ahead.

copywriting--cmp-c3-sc2.prompt: You are writing the button text for an email that offers a free 14-day trial of invoicing software. The goal is trial sign-ups from readers wary of commitment. Which call to action fits best?

options.label: Submit your details to our sales department for follow-up today
Click here to read more about our company and its history
Buy the annual plan now before our prices go up next month
Start my free 14-day trial, no card needed

rubric: The key is action-specific and lowers the perceived risk for wary readers.
Distractors are vague, off-goal, or ask for a bigger commitment than the reader is ready for.

copywriting--exp-c5-sc1.prompt: Two subject lines are tested. Variant A: 20% open rate, 5% of openers click. Variant B: 28% open rate, 3% of openers click. The landing page and purchase rate are identical. The goal is sales per email sent. Which judgement is best?

options.label: Ship B: opens are the earliest funnel step, so the gain compounds into more sales later
Either: the open-rate gain and click-rate loss cancel out, so choose on brand tone
Ship A: it earns 1.0 clicks per 100 sends against 0.84 for B
Ship B: the higher open rate shows its subject line persuades more people to engage

rubric: Sales per send depends on open rate times click rate: 0.20x0.05=1.0% vs 0.28x0.03=0.84%.
Distractors reward opens as a vanity metric or assume the trade-off is neutral.

copywriting--exp-c6-sc1.prompt: Write a headline for an insulated bottle aimed at commuters. Constraints: at most 9 words, states the reader's outcome, contains a concrete number, makes no unprovable superlative. Which meets all four?

options.label: Ice still frozen after 12 hours in your bag
Premium stainless steel keeps your drinks colder for longer
The world's best bottle keeps drinks cold for 12 hours
Double-walled 18/8 stainless steel with a leakproof lid

rubric: It states an outcome, includes a number, uses 9 words and has no superlative.
Distractors break one constraint each: superlative and length, no number, or feature not outcome.

copywriting--nov-c2-sc2.prompt: A product page says 'Only 3 left in stock.' Which persuasion technique is this line using?

options.label: Price anchoring against a higher price
Social proof from other buyers
Scarcity and urgency
Storytelling about the maker

rubric: Limited availability prompts faster action, which is scarcity and urgency.
Social proof relies on others' approval; anchoring compares prices.

copywriting--prf-c5-sc4.prompt: A course seller wants launch urgency. Criteria: protect long-term trust, keep repeat buyers, and still lift conversions. Which approach fits best?

options.label: Use a countdown timer that restarts for each new visitor, since a visible clock lifts conversions on the first visit
Extend the deadline quietly when sales are slow, since late buyers still get the offer and revenue improves
Close enrolment on a real date tied to the cohort start, state why, then honour it
Show "only 3 spots left" on the sales page even if seats are open, since scarcity messaging raises urgency

rubric: A real, explained deadline creates urgency without damaging trust when honoured.
Fake timers, shifting deadlines and invented scarcity erode credibility once noticed.

creative-writing--cmp-c3-sc2.prompt: Tom wants his sister Jo to leave his flat but cannot bring himself to say so. Which line of dialogue applies subtext best?

options.label: "Your train's at six, isn't it? I'll find your coat."
"Please go, Jo, I cannot stand having you here in my flat any longer than this."
"I want you to leave now because I'm exhausted and honestly a bit angry with you."
"I am feeling irritated and would like some time alone to calm myself down."

rubric: Subtext means the real wish is implied by what is said, and the key hints at it through logistics.
The distractors state the desire or emotion outright, which is on-the-nose dialogue.

creative-writing--exp-c5-sc4.prompt: A story's central question is whether a ferry pilot will report her friend's drinking. The draft ends with the friend suddenly inheriting money and moving away. Judged against the criterion that an ending must answer the central question using forces already in the story, what is the main flaw?

options.label: Outside luck removes the choice, so the pilot never decides
The ending never states what the pilot learned about loyalty, so readers must infer the theme without any explicit statement from the narrator
The ending comes too quickly after the climax, so the pilot's emotional reaction to the friend leaving is not given enough space on the page
The ending leaves the friend's future uncertain, so readers cannot know whether the drinking problem was ever resolved after the move

rubric: An ending delivered by coincidence dodges the dramatic question that the protagonist's choice should answer.
Distractors invent rules about length, morals or full closure that are not the stated criterion.

creative-writing--prf-c4-sn1.prompt: A writer finishes a village mystery. In the last chapter the culprit is revealed to be the postman, a character mentioned once on page 9 and never shown in a scene. Beta readers say they felt cheated even though the motive makes sense. What is the best diagnosis?

options.label: The story is narrated in first person, which prevents the reveal from feeling fair to readers of a mystery
The ending is rushed, so adding two more pages of explanation after the reveal would let readers absorb how the culprit's motive developed
The culprit was never planted through scenes or clues, so the reveal feels arbitrary
The motive is too simple, and a more tangled backstory for the postman would make the revelation feel earned and satisfying to readers

rubric: A fair mystery needs earlier setup so the solution feels inevitable in hindsight.
Distractors point at pacing, motive and POV, which are not the source of the cheated feeling.

critical-thinking--adb-c3-sc2.prompt: Premise 1: If it rains, the match is cancelled. Premise 2: The match was not cancelled. Which conclusion follows?

options.label: Nothing can be concluded about the rain
It did not rain
It rained, but the match was played anyway
The weather was sunny all day

rubric: Denying the consequent shows the condition did not occur (modus tollens).
Learners who say nothing follows confuse this with the invalid denial of the antecedent.

critical-thinking--cmp-c4-sc1.prompt: 'Most billionaires dropped out of college, so dropping out is a good route to wealth.' Which flaw best explains why this evidence is weak?

options.label: It attacks college graduates personally instead of addressing the argument that dropping out leads to wealth
It counts only the dropouts who succeeded and ignores the many who did not
It treats wealth as the only measure of a good life, though many people value other outcomes more
It relies on an authority who may be biased toward the conclusion, such as billionaires promoting themselves

rubric: This is survivorship bias: the sample includes only successful cases, so the success rate of dropouts is unknown.
Other options name flaws that are not present in the argument as stated.

customer-service--exp-c6-sc4.prompt: A team proposes this post-incident plan: publish a status page, email all affected customers once the fix is live, and brief agents with a script. What is the most important thing it is missing?

options.label: A public status-page history of past incidents, so future customers can judge how often this kind of failure happens
A compensation promise announced up front, before the incident's real cost to each customer is known
Follow-up on the open cases of customers who already contacted support
A personal apology call from an agent to every affected customer, whatever the size of their impact

rubric: Customers with open cases need follow-up on their own tickets, or they must chase; the plan treats everyone as a generic audience.
Other options are excessive, cosmetic or financially premature.

customer-service--nov-c1-sn1.prompt: A new support agent is told to follow the standard complaint steps. A customer calls upset about a late delivery. The agent wants to recall the usual first step in handling a complaint. Which step is it?

options.label: Transfer the call to a manager who can approve a refund
Explain the company's delivery policy and its stated timelines
Listen to the complaint without interrupting
Offer compensation right away to calm the customer down

rubric: Listening fully comes first so the customer feels heard and the problem is clear.
Jumping to policy, compensation or transfer skips understanding the problem.

customer-service--nov-c2-sc2.prompt: Which reply is the best example of a positive tone in an email to a customer?

options.label: "Per our policy, that is not something we are responsible for here."
"As the policy states, you should have checked this before ordering."
"Unfortunately we can't do anything about that request today."
"I can help with that. Here is what we will do."

rubric: Focusing on what you can do keeps the tone helpful.
The others blame or shut the customer down.

customer-service--prf-c4-sc4.prompt: A customer says a refund promised 'within 5 to 7 business days' hasn't arrived 10 days after they asked. Which detail should the agent check first?

options.label: The customer's tone in the message, since angry customers tend to overstate how long they have been waiting
The size of the customer's bank, since large banks tend to process incoming refunds more slowly than small ones
Whether the customer has contacted support before, since repeat callers often misjudge how long they have waited
The date the refund was issued, since the window may start then, not at the request

rubric: The window runs from issue date, not request date, so the timeline must be reconciled first.
Distractors rely on stereotypes about customers or banks.

data-structures--nov-c2-sc1.prompt: Why is reading `arr[5]` from an array fast regardless of array size?

options.label: The array is scanned from the start until position 5 is reached
The index is looked up in a hash table that maps it to a slot
The address is computed directly from the index
The elements are kept sorted, so position 5 is found by halving

rubric: Contiguous memory lets the address be computed as base plus offset.
Scanning would make access slower for larger arrays.

data-structures--prf-c4-sc4.prompt: A min-heap stored in an array uses 0-based indexing. A developer's `parent(i)` returns `i / 2` with integer division, and the heap property is violated after several inserts. What is the most likely cause?

options.label: Integer division truncates the result, so every parent index comes out too small and sift-up stops after one comparison at most
Sift-up must start at the root and proceed downward, so the direction of the loop is what breaks the heap property over time
With 0-based indexing the parent is `(i - 1) / 2`, so sift-up compares nodes with wrong parents
A min-heap needs its children stored at `2i` and `2i + 1`, so the child formula is what is wrong and not the parent formula

rubric: With 0-based arrays children are 2i+1 and 2i+2, so the parent is (i-1)/2.
Distractors misattribute the fault to truncation, 1-based child formulas or sift direction.

decision-making--cmp-c4-sc4.prompt: Option A pays 100 for certain. Option B has a 90% chance of paying 150 and a 10% chance of losing 100, which the firm could not survive. B's EV is 125. Why can ranking by EV alone mislead here?

options.label: A 10% chance is small enough to treat as negligible, so EV overstates the danger in B and A should not be preferred
EV averages over many repeats, but the firm faces a one-off loss it cannot survive
EV weights outcomes by probability, so it counts the 10% loss too heavily when the payoffs differ this much
EV is defined only for outcomes that are certain, so a gamble like B cannot be evaluated with it at all

rubric: EV assumes repeated plays; with a ruinous outcome, survival matters more than the average.
Other options misdescribe what EV does.

decision-making--cmp-c4-sn1.prompt: A manager funds launches using expected value. The team rates every launch 90% likely to hit target, yet past records show only 60% of launches did. EV rankings keep favouring launches that then disappoint. What is the best diagnosis and fix?

options.label: Probabilities are unreliable in principle, so drop EV and rank launches by cost alone, which is easier to measure
The EV method is flawed, so replace it with the judgment of the most senior member, who has seen the most launches
The team is overconfident, so pull estimates toward the 60% base rate and track results
The team is right to be optimistic, since past launches differ from these, so keep the 90% estimates and re-run EV

rubric: Persistent gaps between stated and historical success point to overconfidence; base rates and feedback recalibrate estimates.
Other options abandon the method or dismiss the evidence.

decision-making--nov-c2-sc5.prompt: Why is it a mistake to continue a failing project mainly because of the money already spent on it?

options.label: Past spending shows the project is close to paying off, so quitting now would waste the chance of a return
That money is gone whichever option you pick, so it should not decide the choice
Stopping is always better than continuing once costs have started to pile up past the original budget
Money already spent should be counted again as a cost of stopping, so it tilts the comparison toward continuing

rubric: Sunk costs are identical across options, so only future costs and benefits should count.
Distractors invert the logic or claim stopping is always better.

deep-learning--adb-c2-sn1.prompt: A team removes positional encodings from a small transformer for translation. Afterwards the model produces nearly the same output for "dog bites man" and "man bites dog". Why does this happen?

options.label: Word embeddings are looked up from a fixed table, so they lose the order in which the words were typed
The softmax in attention spreads weight so evenly across the words that each word's own meaning is blurred
Self-attention has no sense of word order, so order information is lost
Attention heads mostly compare words that sit near each other, so distant word order gets ignored

rubric: Self-attention treats tokens as a set; positional encodings supply order.
Attention is not limited to adjacent words and weights are not forced to be equal.

design-patterns--prf-c5-sc4.prompt: A data sink offers optional compression, encryption, buffering and logging, chosen per deployment at runtime in any combination and order. Criteria: no class explosion, features testable independently, configurable order. Which design is best?

options.label: Decorators sharing the sink interface, composed at startup in the configured order.
A subclass for every combination of features, because inheritance keeps each variant's behavior explicit and testable.
One sink class with four boolean flags, because a single class is simplest and the flags choose features per deployment.
A Template Method base with a hook per feature, overridden by one subclass for each deployment configuration.

rubric: Decorators compose independent features in any order without a combinatorial class count.
Subclasses explode, flags fix the order, and Template Method needs a subclass per configuration.

differential-calculus--adb-c2-sc3.prompt: Let f(x) = (x^2 - 4)/(x - 2) for x not equal to 2. What is true about the limit of f(x) as x approaches 2?

options.label: It equals 0, because the numerator x^2 - 4 is zero when x = 2 and so f(x) tends to zero
It equals 2, because the denominator x - 2 simplifies to 2 at that point and the factor cancels
It does not exist, because f(2) is undefined so no value can be approached from either side
It equals 4, because f(x) = x + 2 for x not equal to 2

rubric: For x not equal to 2, f(x) = x + 2, so values approach 4; the limit ignores the value at 2.
Distractors assume a limit needs f(2) to be defined or substitute incorrectly.

differential-equations--cmp-c4-sn1.prompt: A fish population follows `P' = 0.5P(1 - P/200) - 20`, where 20 is the harvest per year. Setting P' = 0 gives equilibria near 55.3 and 144.7. The upper one is stable and the lower one is unstable. A disease drops the population to 40. What does the model predict?

options.label: The population oscillates around the unstable equilibrium at 55.3
The population declines to zero in finite time
The population rises and settles at the unstable equilibrium near 55.3
The population recovers to the stable level of about 144.7

rubric: Below the unstable equilibrium the net growth rate is negative, so P decreases and the fishery collapses.
A first-order autonomous equation cannot oscillate, and 55.3 repels nearby solutions.

digital-marketing--prf-c5-sc3.prompt: A colleague proposes pausing all brand-term search ads because the company already ranks first organically for them. Judged on protecting revenue and spending efficiently, which response is best?

options.label: Approve it, because an organic first-place result usually captures the brand clicks and the paid ads mostly duplicate it, so the saved budget is better spent elsewhere
Reject it, because brand ads help Quality Score on non-brand keywords, so pausing them would probably raise costs across the whole account
Run a holdout test pausing brand ads in some regions, since competitors may bid on the brand name
Approve it if the company's ads never name competitors, because competitor bidding on the brand is then the only risk to revenue

rubric: Incrementality of brand ads is uncertain and testable; a holdout measures real lost clicks and revenue.
Distractors assume full organic capture or invent an absolute rule.

discrete-mathematics--cmp-c4-sc1.prompt: A proof claims every integer n >= 1 satisfies P(n) by showing P(1) and 'if P(k) then P(k+1) for k >= 2'. What is wrong?

options.label: The base case must be P(0), since induction on integers always starts at zero
The step never links P(1) to P(2), so the chain is broken
The hypothesis must assume all P(j) for j < k, because plain P(k) is too weak
One base case is not enough, since the step needs two starting values proven

rubric: The inductive step starts at k=2, leaving P(2) unproven.
Other options misdiagnose the gap.

discrete-mathematics--exp-c6-sc1.prompt: You will prove by strong induction that every integer n >= 12 equals 4a + 5b with a, b >= 0. The step writes n as (n-4) + 4 and uses the claim for n-4. Which is the smallest set of base cases that makes the proof complete?

options.label: 12 through 16, since the step needs n-4 >= 12
12 only, since the step then reaches every larger n
12 and 13, since 4 and 5 differ by one

rubric: The step reaches back four, so it is valid only for n >= 16; the four values 12 to 15 must be checked directly.
Fewer bases leave gaps; 16 is already covered by the step.

options.label: Reflexive: (1,3) is missing, so not every element is related to every element of the set
Symmetric: (1,3) is absent, so some related pair lacks its reversed partner in the relation
Transitive: (1,2) and (2,3) are in R, but (1,3) is not
Antisymmetric is required: (1,2) and (2,1) both appear, so R is not a valid relation at all

rubric: Chaining 1R2 and 2R3 requires 1R3, which is absent, so transitivity fails.
R is reflexive and symmetric; a missing pair in both directions does not break symmetry.

drawing--adb-c3-sc2.prompt: You draw a box in one-point perspective with its front face toward you. Which statement about the edges of the front face is correct?

options.label: Its top and bottom edges both stay exactly horizontal
None stay horizontal, since every edge must tilt toward the vanishing point
Only the bottom edge stays horizontal, since it rests on the ground plane and the top tilts
Its top and bottom edges both slope toward the vanishing point on the horizon

rubric: In one-point perspective, the face parallel to the picture plane keeps true horizontals and verticals.
Distractors apply convergence to the front face or favour one edge.

drawing--cmp-c3-sc3.prompt: A single light source sits high and to the upper left of a sphere resting on a flat table. Where do you draw the cast shadow?

options.label: On the sphere itself, as a band along its upper left edge facing the light
On the table to the upper left, beneath the light and set apart from the sphere
On the table directly beneath the sphere, as a small circle hidden behind it
On the table to the lower right, touching the sphere's base

rubric: Cast shadows fall on the opposite side of the object from the light and connect at the contact point.
Placing the shadow on the light side confuses cast shadow with highlight or form shadow.

drawing--cmp-c4-sc2.prompt: In a frontal portrait the face looks wrong, as if the features were pasted high on the head. The eyes sit close to the top of the skull outline. What construction error best explains this?

options.label: The eyes sit above the head's midpoint, leaving too little skull above
The chin was drawn too narrow and short, which compresses the lower half of the face and pushes the mouth and nose upward
The ears were aligned with the brow and nose instead of set lower, which pulls the whole feature set up toward the crown
The nose was placed too close to the mouth, so the lower face looks short and the features seem to crowd upward

rubric: The eyes sit roughly halfway down the head, and placing them near the top leaves features crowded high.
Ear, nose and chin faults produce different distortions.

drawing--exp-c5-sc1.prompt: A tonal drawing of a still life has accurate shapes, but it looks flat because every edge is equally sharp and dark. Judged by the criterion of convincing depth, which revision is best?

options.label: Raise the contrast across the whole sheet so the darkest darks and lightest lights appear in every area of the drawing
Vary edge quality, crisp at the focal point and softer or lost elsewhere
Add hatching texture to the surfaces so that the materials are identified and each object reads as distinct
Darken the outlines of the forms nearest the viewer so that each one separates clearly from its neighbours

rubric: Varying edge sharpness (lost and found edges) creates atmosphere and a focal hierarchy.
Uniform lines, texture or contrast flatten the image because nothing recedes.

drawing--nov-c1-sc1.prompt: In a perspective drawing, what does the horizon line represent?

options.label: The edge of the paper's frame
The lightest area of the scene
The viewer's eye level
The ground under the nearest object

rubric: The horizon line marks the viewer's eye level.
Distractors confuse it with the ground, value or the page edge.

options.label: The darkest spot in a shaded area, where light is blocked
The point where the horizon line meets the edge of the paper
Where parallel receding lines appear to meet
The centre point of the paper, where all lines must cross

rubric: Parallel lines receding from the viewer appear to converge at a vanishing point.
Distractors confuse it with shading or the page centre.

ecology--adb-c2-sn1.prompt: Fertilizer runoff from nearby farms enters a small lake. Within weeks the surface is covered in algae, and later many fish are found dead. A student wants to explain the fish deaths. Which explanation is best?

options.label: Dead algae were decomposed by bacteria, which used up the dissolved oxygen
The extra nutrients from the fertilizer poisoned the fish directly when they swallowed the contaminated water
The algae released so much extra oxygen that the water became toxic to the fish's gills over time
A thick algal mat blocked all the sunlight, so fish could no longer see well enough to find food

rubric: Eutrophication leads to algal die-off, and bacterial decomposition depletes oxygen.
Distractors suggest direct poisoning, vision problems or oxygen excess.

ecology--cmp-c4-sc4.prompt: On a rocky shore, barnacle species A lives only in the upper zone. When competitor species B is removed from the lower zone, A also colonises the lower zone and survives. What does this show?

options.label: Competition from B restricts A's realised niche
A is physically unable to tolerate the lower zone's conditions while B is present
B facilitates A by providing shelter from wave action in the upper zone
The upper zone is A's fundamental niche, so its range cannot expand

rubric: Expansion after competitor removal shows the realised niche was smaller than the fundamental niche.
The other options ignore the removal result.

ecology--prf-c5-sn1.prompt: A manager estimates a fish stock's carrying capacity at 100,000 t with logistic growth, so maximum sustainable yield occurs near a stock of 50,000 t. The estimate is highly uncertain, and earlier overestimates led to collapse. Criteria: sustain yield and avoid collapse. Which policy is best?

options.label: Close the fishery until carrying capacity is measured exactly, since any harvest under uncertainty risks collapse
Set quotas at the estimated MSY level, since it maximises yield and errors in the estimate are equally likely in both directions
Set quotas below the estimated MSY and adjust them as monitoring narrows the uncertainty
Keep the stock near estimated carrying capacity, since the largest population always gives the largest long-term harvest

rubric: A precautionary, adaptive quota keeps yield while buffering against overestimated capacity.
Harvesting at the estimated MSY ignores asymmetric collapse risk, yield is near zero at K, and a total closure sacrifices yield unnecessarily.

electrical-circuits--nov-c2-sc2.prompt: Two resistors are connected in series. How does the current through them compare?

options.label: It is larger through the smaller resistor
It is split in proportion to resistance
It is larger through the bigger resistor
It is the same through both

rubric: Series elements share one path, so current is identical.
Splitting current is behavior of parallel branches.

electrical-circuits--prf-c5-sn1.prompt: A team picks a fuse for a 12 V circuit that normally draws 3 A with 10 A startup surges lasting 50 ms. Criteria: protect wiring rated 8 A continuous, and avoid nuisance blowing. Which fuse is best?

options.label: A 7.5 A slow-blow fuse, tolerating brief surges but protecting the wire
A 15 A fast-acting fuse, since it clears the 10 A surge with margin and still limits fault current
A 20 A slow-blow fuse, since it rides through surges and gives margin for all load conditions
A 3 A fast-acting fuse, since it matches the running current and gives the tightest protection

rubric: Slow-blow tolerates surges and 7.5 A is below the wire limit.
Others nuisance-trip or exceed wire rating.

electricity-and-magnetism--adb-c2-sc1.prompt: Two small like charges repel each other with force F. The distance between them is doubled and the charges are unchanged. What happens to the force?

options.label: It doubles, because the force grows with separation
It stays equal to F, because the charges are unchanged
It falls to one quarter of F
It falls to one half of F, because force goes as 1/r

rubric: Coulomb's force varies as 1/r^2, so doubling r gives F/4.
Choosing one half treats the force as inversely proportional to distance, not distance squared.

electricity-and-magnetism--adb-c2-sc5.prompt: A positive charge moves in a straight line parallel to a uniform magnetic field. What magnetic force acts on it?

options.label: Zero, since only the velocity component across the field counts
Maximum, since the charge moves along the field direction and feels the full field strength
Opposite its motion, since the field slows moving charges by acting like a drag force
Along its motion, since the field pushes a positive charge the way the field points

rubric: The magnetic force is q v x B, which vanishes when v is parallel to B.
Magnetic forces are perpendicular to velocity and do no work, so they never speed up or slow a charge.

electricity-and-magnetism--nov-c2-sc3.prompt: What does the magnetic field around a long straight wire carrying current look like?

options.label: Closed circles around the wire
No field exists unless the wire is coiled
Straight lines running parallel to the wire
Lines pointing radially outward from the wire

rubric: The field forms closed circles around the wire, with direction given by the right-hand rule.
Radial lines describe an electric field of a charged wire, and coiling only strengthens the field.

emotional-intelligence--adb-c3-sc3.prompt: Your heart is racing ten minutes before a presentation. Which technique best calms your body?

options.label: Breathe in for four counts and out for six, for a minute
Tell yourself firmly to stop feeling nervous right now, and repeat it until the feeling fades
Speed-read your slides again to burn off the nervous energy before you start
Drink a strong coffee so that you feel more alert and focused when you begin

rubric: Slow breathing with a longer exhale lowers physical arousal.
Distractors suppress the feeling or add stimulation and pressure.

engineering-mechanics--prf-c4-sc1.prompt: At joint D of a plane truss, members DA and DB are collinear and horizontal, and member DC rises at 40° above horizontal. A 5 kN external load acts horizontally at D. What is the force in DC?

options.label: 5 / cos 40° kN
5 tan 40° kN
Zero
5 sin 40° kN

rubric: Summing forces perpendicular to the collinear members gives F_DC sin 40° = 0, so DC carries nothing.
Distractors apply the load to DC as though the collinear members could not absorb a horizontal load.

entrepreneurship--cmp-c4-sc1.prompt: A landing page got 2,000 visitors and 60 free-trial sign-ups (3%), but none of the 60 converted to paid after the trial. What is the most likely explanation to test first?

options.label: The 3% sign-up rate is too small a sample to mean anything, so the test should be repeated with 20,000 visitors before drawing any conclusion
The product lacks features, so the next step is to build the most requested ones and then rerun the same free trial for a new cohort
Free sign-ups measured curiosity, not willingness to pay, so demand was weaker than it looked
Trial users typically churn at the end of any free period, so zero paid conversions is within normal range and the offer needs no change

rubric: Free sign-ups are a weak proxy; zero paid conversions suggests no proven willingness to pay.
Distractors blame sample size, normalise churn or assume features without diagnosing the signal.

entrepreneurship--nov-c2-sc4.prompt: A new bakery spends more each month than it earns and has no other funding. What is most likely to happen eventually?

options.label: It will run out of cash and be unable to operate
Costs will shrink by themselves as the bakery gets established
Customers will accept higher prices once the bakery has been open a while
Sales will rise as word spreads about the bakery's low profits

rubric: Spending more than earning without funding drains cash until the business cannot operate.
Distractors assume costs, prices or sales will correct themselves automatically.

epidemiology--exp-c5-sn1.prompt: After a banquet of 60 guests, 24 became ill. Of 30 who ate the potato salad, 22 were ill; of 30 who did not, 2 were ill. Of 50 who ate the chicken, 23 were ill; of 10 who did not, 1 was ill. Which judgement about the likely vehicle is best supported?

options.label: Both equally, as each shows a higher attack rate in the exposed than in the unexposed guests, so neither can be ranked
Neither, because with only 60 guests no difference in attack rates between foods can be told apart from chance
Potato salad, since its risk ratio is about 11 and few unexposed guests fell ill
Chicken, because 23 of the 24 ill guests ate it, so it accounts for almost every case in the outbreak

rubric: Salad attack rate 73% vs 7% (RR about 11) versus chicken 46% vs 10% (RR about 4.6); most chicken eaters also ate salad.
Chicken has the most ill eaters only because nearly everyone ate it.

epidemiology--nov-c2-sc3.prompt: Researchers enroll 5,000 smokers and non-smokers free of lung cancer and follow them for 10 years, recording who develops it. How is this study best classified?

options.label: Case series report
Case-control study
Cross-sectional survey study
Cohort study

rubric: Following exposed and unexposed groups forward in time is a cohort design.
Case-control studies begin with outcome status, not exposure.

evolution--exp-c5-sc5.prompt: A genome scan between two stickleback populations finds Fst peaks mainly in low-recombination regions, and the authors claim each peak marks local adaptation. Which critique is strongest?

options.label: Low-recombination regions accumulate mutations faster, which lowers Fst there, so the peaks understate how much local adaptation occurred.
Fst is a relative measure that is noisy at small sample sizes, so peaks in any region are mostly sampling artefacts and not real differences.
Gene flow between the populations raises Fst in low-recombination regions, so the peaks reflect recent migration and not local selection.
Background selection lowers diversity in low-recombination regions and inflates Fst without local adaptation.

rubric: Background selection and sweeps reduce local diversity, raising Fst in low-recombination regions regardless of local adaptation.
Distractors reverse the effect of gene flow on Fst or dismiss Fst as pure noise.

financial-statement-analysis--cmp-c4-sc4.prompt: A firm's operating margin is stable, but its net margin fell sharply. Revenue and gross margin are unchanged. Which line item is the most logical place to look first?

options.label: Selling, general and administrative expenses
Gross profit after any change in inventory costs
Cost of goods sold, including any supplier price changes
Interest expense and taxes

rubric: Stable operating margin means the decline arose below operating income.
COGS, selling expenses and gross profit are above that line.
